## Market Analyses

The global cross-laminated timber market is structurally defined by its dependence on regional softwood supply chains and building-code adoption cycles, which fragment demand across otherwise comparable construction economies. This fragmentation persists because CLT panels require high-grade spruce or pine laminations from managed northern forests, and their load-bearing certification is governed by jurisdiction-specific standards rather than a single global norm. Graphfolio's coverage of production, trade, and per-capita consumption across these regulatory zones lets buyers isolate where code acceptance, rather than raw material cost, is the binding constraint on market penetration.

 Global apparent consumption of cross-laminated timber reached 1.81 million cubic meters in 2025, up 4.0% on 2024 but still below the 2021 peak of 2.05 million cubic meters, according to Graphfolio's market research. Cross-laminated timber consumption is forecast to expand only 3.9% over 2025-2035, reaching 1.88 million cubic meters at a CAGR of +0.4%.

## Why This Data Matters

Procurement teams at mass-timber fabricators track regional production against import volumes to decide whether to source CLT panels from domestic mills or overseas suppliers when lead times tighten. Structural engineers and developers compare consumption per capita across markets to determine whether a project's specified panel thickness can be secured from local inventory or requires advance import contracting.

The economics of CLT hinge on the co-product relationship between lamstock and lower-value lumber grades, meaning panel output competes for the same sawlog input as dimensional framing and can be curtailed without warning when construction framing demand bids up log prices. On the demand side, the material's viability is capped by the fire-rating and acoustic-testing protocols of mid-rise building codes, which impose minimum panel thicknesses that raise timber volume per square meter beyond what structural loads alone would require. Graphfolio's trade and production coverage shows how this dual constraint turns export availability into a residual of domestic framing cycles rather than an independent supply decision.
